reason: The provided sources contain more than 10 highly consistent, multi-sourced claims detailing the 1991 Oh-My-God particle, its extreme energy, and its mysterious origin.
story: On October 15, 1991, an invisible visitor from deep space slammed into Earth's atmosphere, shattering our understanding of physics. Dubbed the 'Oh-My-God' particle, this single subatomic entity carried a staggering 320 exaelectronvolts of energy—equivalent to a baseball flying at 63 miles per hour, or 47 million times the energy of protons inside the Large Hadron Collider. Traveling at 99.9999999999999999999995% the speed of light, it should have been slowed down by the cosmic microwave background, meaning its source had to be relatively nearby. Yet, when scientists traced the particle's path, they found absolutely nothing. This mind-bending cosmic mystery was recently compounded in 2021 by the Amaterasu particle, another ultra-high-energy cosmic ray that emerged from an empty void. These rare cosmic missiles prove that deep space harbors terrifyingly powerful engines we still cannot see.
angle: A single subatomic particle packed the kinetic energy of a fast-pitched baseball, traveling so close to the speed of light that a photon would take over 240,000 years to gain a mere 1-centimeter lead on it.

claims.claim: The Oh-My-God particle was detected on October 15, 1991.
The particle was detected by the Fly's Eye detector in Utah.
The energy of the Oh-My-God particle was estimated to be 320 exaelectronvolts (or 3.2 x 10^20 electronvolts).
The kinetic energy of this single subatomic particle was equivalent to a baseball traveling at roughly 90 to 100 kilometers per hour (about 63 miles per hour).
The particle carried approximately 51 joules of kinetic energy.
The Oh-My-God particle is the highest-energy cosmic ray ever observed.
Assuming the particle was a proton, it was traveling at approximately 99.9999999999999999999995% the speed of light.
The exact composition of the particle remains unknown, though scientists suspect it was either a proton or a heavier nucleus like iron.
The particle's energy was millions of times greater than the maximum energy produced in human-built particle accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider.
Cosmic microwave background radiation limits how far such high-energy cosmic rays can travel before losing energy (known as the GZK limit or cutoff).
Because of the GZK limit, the Oh-My-God particle must have originated relatively nearby in our cosmic neighborhood.
Tracing the arrival direction of the Oh-My-God particle pointed to no obvious astronomical source or accelerator.
Magnetic fields in space deflect charged particles, which bends their trajectory and makes tracing their origin difficult.
In 2021, another ultra-high-energy cosmic ray named the Amaterasu particle was detected with an energy of approximately 240 exaelectronvolts.
The Amaterasu particle appeared to emerge from the Local Void, an empty region of space bordering the Milky Way.

disputed: Sources offer varying macroscopic sports comparisons for the Oh-My-God particle's energy: S1 and S7 describe it as a baseball at 100 km/h (63 mph), S3 describes it as a baseball at 90 km/h, S2 as a slow curveball, and S5 as a fast-bowled cricket ball. The script should generalise this as the kinetic energy of a fast-thrown baseball or cricket ball.

While S3 presents a specific model suggesting almost all extragalactic cosmic rays come from Centaurus A, S5 and S6 emphasize that their exact origin remains an open, highly debated mystery with no consensus. The script should treat their origin as an unsolved mystery while mentioning black hole jets as possible candidate engines.
